test.title: What happens to the clothes we give away

texts.title: What happens to the clothes we give away

paragraphs.text: A bag of clothes left outside a charity shop feels like the end of a story. It is closer to the beginning. Of the garments collected in wealthy countries, only a small share is sold in the shop that received them; the rest enters a trade that sorts, bales and ships used clothing around the world, employs hundreds of thousands of people and is almost entirely invisible to the person who filled the bag.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Sorting is the heart of it and is done by hand. A worker picks up a garment, judges fabric, brand, season and damage in about two seconds, and drops it into one of dozens of streams: sale in the shop, export grade one, export grade two, cleaning cloth, fibre for insulation, waste. The speed is possible because the decision is mostly about the feel of the cloth rather than the label, and the accuracy of that judgement determines whether the bale is worth more than the cost of moving it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The economics have got harder. Clothing is cheaper and thinner than it was twenty years ago, so more of what arrives is worth nothing at the sorting table, while the cost of collection, transport and labour has risen. Several large collectors now describe textile collection as a cost to be covered rather than a source of income, and a few municipalities that once received payment for collected clothing now pay to have it taken away. The trade continues because the good third still pays for the bad two thirds.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Exported clothing has become politically contested, and the argument is not simple. Traders in importing countries buy bales unseen, employ people to open, sort and repair them, and sell garments at prices that local incomes can meet; markets in several West African and East African cities are built on this. Critics point to the share of each bale that is unsellable on arrival, which ends in rivers and open dumps because the importing city has no waste system capable of handling it, and to domestic tailoring industries that cannot compete with cheap imports.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Both things are true at once, which is why bans have produced mixed results. Where imports were restricted, local manufacturing did not automatically revive, because the factories, the fabric supply and the skilled workers had gone; prices of clothing rose, and traders who had employed thousands lost their businesses. The measures that appear to work are duller than a ban: quality thresholds enforced at the port, fees on the exporting side that pay for waste handling on the importing side, and contracts that specify what a bale may contain.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Recycling, in the sense most people imagine, barely exists. Turning old clothing back into new clothing requires separating fibres, and most garments are blends; a cotton-polyester shirt cannot be pulled apart by any process that is currently cheap. What is called recycling is usually downcycling: shredding cloth into insulation, wiping rags or mattress filling, which is useful and is not a circle. Chemical processes that genuinely separate blended fibres exist at pilot scale, and the honest description of them is promising and small.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The clearest lever is upstream. A garment worn thirty times instead of ten has, by that fact alone, a third of the impact per wearing, and no sorting system can achieve anything comparable. This is awkward for everyone involved: for brands whose revenue depends on volume, for charities whose income depends on donations, and for consumers who have been told that giving clothes away is itself a virtuous act. It is easier to improve a supply chain than to buy less, which is one reason so much attention goes to the end of the pipe.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What would help the sorting trade is information. A label that recorded fibre content reliably, and a design that allowed a garment to be taken apart, would raise the value of what arrives at the table and reduce what is thrown away behind it. Several jurisdictions are now drafting rules of exactly this kind, with fees on producers that rise for garments that are hard to recycle. Whether that changes what is made, rather than adding a cost that is passed to the buyer, is the question the next decade will answer.
paragraphs.label: H

topic.en: What the text is about: what happens to donated clothing — sorting, export, the argument about bans, and why true recycling is still rare.

topic.ru: О чём текст: что происходит с отданной одеждой — сортировка, экспорт, спор о запретах и почему настоящая переработка пока редкость.

explanation.ru: Абзац B — про саму сортировку: две секунды на вещь и десятки потоков → i.

explanation.en: Paragraph C is about money: clothing is cheaper, costs are up, collection is now an expense → ii.
explanation.kk: C абзацы ақша туралы: киім арзандайды, шығын өседі, жинау шығынға айналды → ii.
explanation.ru: Абзац C — про деньги: одежда дешевеет, расходы растут, сбор стал статьёй затрат → ii.

explanation.ru: Абзац D даёт обе стороны спора об экспорте: рабочие места и рынки против свалок и местных портных → iv.
